nameStory: The sei whale gets its name from the Norwegian word for pollock fish, "seje." Norwegian fishermen noticed that these whales would arrive in their coastal waters at the same time as schools of pollock, making them a reliable sign that fishing season had begun.
description: The sei whale is a massive ocean giant and the third-largest whale species in the world. These sleek marine mammals can stretch up to 64 feet long and weigh as much as 31 tons - imagine a school bus that's been stretched to twice its length! They have a dark steel-gray body with a streamlined shape built for speed, making them among the fastest whales in the ocean.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Enormous streamlined body up to 64 feet long with a tall, curved dorsal fin located about two-thirds back from the head. The whale appears sleek and torpedo-shaped when seen from a distance.

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Dark steel-gray body that looks almost metallic in sunlight, with sporadic light gray to white markings on the belly. The uniform dark coloring distinguishes it from other large whales.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Incredibly fast swimmer that can reach speeds of 31-34 mph, often seen skimming just below the surface. Usually travels alone or in small groups of up to six individuals.

idTips.label: Feeding Sign
idTips.description: Look for areas of disturbed water where the whale has been filter-feeding on tiny copepods and krill. May see scattered small crustaceans and a slightly oily sheen on the water's surface.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found only in deep offshore waters of the open ocean, avoiding shallow coastal areas, polar waters, and enclosed bays. Prefers the continental shelf edge and beyond.

habitat: Sei whales inhabit the deep offshore waters of the North Atlantic, far from New England's coastline. They prefer the open ocean beyond the continental shelf, typically in waters thousands of feet deep where their tiny prey congregates.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in New England offshore waters as they migrate north from warmer winter grounds. Most likely to be spotted during organized whale watching expeditions to deep water areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sei whale sightings in New England waters as they follow concentrations of copepods and krill in the cool, nutrient-rich northern waters.
seasonality.fall: Still present in offshore waters but beginning to move south toward warmer winter territories. Groups may be slightly larger during this migration period.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters as they migrate to temperate and subtropical regions to breed and give birth.

funFact: Sei whales are the speed demons of the whale world - they can rocket through the water at over 30 mph, making them faster than most boats and earning them the nickname 'the greyhound of the sea.'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with fin whales, but sei whales are smaller, uniformly dark gray (fin whales have asymmetrical jaw coloring), and have a more curved dorsal fin. Remember: 'Sei' rhymes with 'gray' - they're the uniformly gray ones.
contextualKnowledge: Sei whales are extremely rare to spot from shore in New England due to their preference for deep offshore waters. The 19 recorded observations likely represent decades of dedicated offshore whale research and deep-water whale watching expeditions.
compareHints: Compared to their close relatives, sei whales are smaller than fin whales but larger than minke whales. Unlike fin whales which have distinctive asymmetrical white jaw patches, sei whales maintain their uniform dark steel-gray coloring. They're also much faster swimmers than either relative, and prefer deeper offshore waters than the more coastal minke whales.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to their close relative the common minke whale, fin whales are dramatically larger (minkes max out around 30 feet versus fin whales' 85+ feet) and have much more prominent dorsal fins.
Compared to their larger rorqual relatives in New England waters, minke whales are much smaller and more agile than fin whales, which can reach 70 feet and have asymmetrical jaw coloring.
